source.title: Tracing the Thought of a Grandmaster-level Chess-Playing Transformer
source.authors: Rui Lin; Zhenyu Jin; Guan-Chen Zhou; Xuyang Ge; Wentao Shu; Jiaxing Wu; Junxuan Wang; Zheng-Fu He; Junping Zhang; Xi-Peng Qiu

record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse replacement layers to interpret the model, motivated in part by superposition and the stated uninterpretablity of individual neurons, but does not test the listed polysemanticity claims.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports human ratings of activation consistency and complexity for MLP neurons and sparse replacement features. These results concern interpretability in a chess model, but do not measure unrelated neuron responses or test any listed version. Other reported results concern feature-level pathways, interventions, and path metrics; cited findings from prior work are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study decomposes a chess transformer (LC0 BT4) with Transcoders and Lorsas. It states without testing that neurons are uninterpretable because of superposition. Its only neuron-level result is a small human rating (Table 1): 3 raters on a 1–5 scale comparing MLP neurons with its own sparse features. That is a chess transformer, not an image classifier (V1) or a language model (V2). It does not test causes (V3, V4), architecture effects (V5), reinterpretation of canonical neurons (V6) or measurement choices (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that sparse replacement layers (Transcoders for MLPs, Lorsas for attention) yield interpretable features and reasoning pathways, validated by interventions, that expose LC0's tactical reasoning. They also report that the model reasons through largely parallel, disjoint pathways for candidate moves, and that move-relevant information converges on source and target squares in deeper layers. They note that some features remain hard to interpret and that the work covers one architecture.
record.recipe_differences: This is a sparse-decomposition and circuit-tracing study using Transcoders for MLPs and Lorsas for attention, with feature-steering interventions; it is not a reproduction of the cited original sources' methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Three chess-player raters scored LC0 BT4 MLP neurons at 2.05/5 for activation consistency, against 4.15 for Transcoder features and 3.73 for Lorsa features. Neurons also scored lower on perceived complexity (1.45 vs 2.25 and 2.54). No uncertainty is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a chess-playing transformer trained by self-play RL, human raters judge individual MLP neurons' activations less consistent (more mixed) than sparse-dictionary features.

record.problems: The human interpretability assessment uses three annotators and reports no uncertainty for its scores. The study examines only one architecture, and its ratings do not directly test whether individual neurons activate for unrelated inputs.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing directly on the listed versions were reported. Other results on feature pathways, chess moves, and path metrics were omitted because they do not measure neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: No language models are studied. Low neuron consistency is shown only in a chess transformer, with no per-layer share of polysemantic neurons.
Superposition is invoked as motivation only; capacity pressure is not tested.
Initialization, regularization and training noise are not examined.
One architecture only; activation functions and regularization are not varied.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
No comparison of activation ranges or scoring methods for neurons. The study does use a 10%-of-maximum activation threshold for its feature validation.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation (assumes) and tranche (T4) hold. Table 1 is the only neuron-level evidence: a rubric rating in a non-language, non-vision transformer, with 3 annotators and no uncertainty. It therefore links to no version. The fits_no_version wording 'less complexly interpretable' was corrected: a lower complexity score means the neurons' patterns were perceived as simpler, not less interpretable.

versions.untested_parts: The study examines a chess transformer, not image classifiers, and does not test individual neurons' responses to multiple unrelated inputs.
No language models, tokens, or language contexts are studied.
The study invokes superposition as motivation but does not test whether feature-neuron capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
The study does not test polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
It studies one architecture and does not compare activation functions, architectures, or regularization settings for their effects on neuron polysemanticity.
It does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons or establish that their mixed responses reflect one shared feature or related jobs.
It does not compare activation-range choices or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons as polysemantic.
